name: Tautology / Contradiction / Satisfiability / Truth-Value Determination
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek formula di hai aur poocha hai ye tautology hai, contradiction hai, satisfiable hai, ya specific truth-value poocha hai (given kuch propositions ka value) — ye is topic ka sabse bada pattern hai (40 me se 21 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: ≤3 variables → truth table banao seedha, 8 rows se zyada nahi honge, guaranteed correct.
Try the implication-rewrite (P→Q ≡ ¬P∨Q) first to simplify before building a table.
'Satisfiable but not valid' = TRUE for SOME rows, FALSE for others (neither tautology nor contradiction).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Count distinct propositional variables (n) — if n≤3, default to a full truth table (fast, safe).
2. If n is larger or the formula looks algebraically simplifiable, rewrite all → and ↔ into ∧/∨/¬ form first using the rewrite rules.
3. Apply De Morgan's/distributive laws to simplify.
4. Classify: all-True rows → tautology; all-False → contradiction; mixed → satisfiable-but-not-valid.
5. For 'given P is true, find truth value of complex formula' — substitute directly rather than building the whole table.
variationsObserved: Given that two OTHER formulas are tautologies, deduce properties of a formula built from them (meta-reasoning, not direct truth-table).
'True when exactly two of P,Q,R are true' — build the table but only check the specific 3-of-8 rows matching that condition.
Given a formula is a CONTRADICTION, deduce the truth value/status of a related formula (reverse-engineering).
commonTraps: Missing that P→Q is vacuously true when P is False — leads to wrong row entries.
Confusing 'satisfiable' (true in at least one row) with 'valid/tautology' (true in ALL rows) — these are different claims.
edgeCases: Formula with 0 free variables after simplification (constant True/False) — trivial classification.

name: Logical Equivalence Verification (which formulas mean the same thing)
recognitionClueHinglish: Do ya zyada formulas diye hain aur poocha hai kaunse equivalent hain (same truth table) — ye equivalence-matching pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Rewrite every candidate formula into a canonical ∧/∨/¬ form (kill → and ↔ first) — then compare directly.
If algebra gets messy, fall back to a truth table and compare COLUMNS across all candidates at once (more efficient than pairwise for multiple options).
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Pick the 'target' formula (the one others are compared against).
3. For each candidate option, rewrite similarly and compare structurally, OR build one combined truth table with a column per candidate.
variationsObserved: Custom binary operator defined by a truth table, asked which standard expression matches it.
commonTraps: Assuming converse or inverse is equivalent to the original conditional — only contrapositive is guaranteed equivalent.

name: Natural Language ↔ Propositional Logic Translation
recognitionClueHinglish: English statement diya hai (jaise 'P only if Q', 'P unless Q', 'I stay only if you go') aur poocha hai correct formula/converse/representation kaunsa hai — ye translation pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: 'P if and only if Q' → P↔Q.
Converse of P→Q is Q→P; contrapositive is ¬Q→¬P; inverse is ¬P→¬Q — only contrapositive is logically equivalent to the original.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Underline the connective keywords in the English sentence (only if / if / unless / and / or / not / iff).
2. Assign a propositional variable to each atomic claim.
3. Assemble using the keyword-to-connective mapping above.
4. If asked for converse/inverse/contrapositive of a given assertion, apply the specific transformation rather than re-deriving from English.
variationsObserved: Compound sentence with multiple nested connectives ('P and Q, and not R only if S and T') — parse left-to-right, identify the OUTERMOST connective first.
commonTraps: 'Only if' vs 'if' direction swap — the single most common translation error.
Missing an implicit NOT in phrases like 'P cannot be given when Q'.

name: Logical Inference / Argument Validity (Modus Ponens, Resolution)
recognitionClueHinglish: Premises di hain aur ek conclusion validate/derive karna hai, ya 'which arguments are valid' poocha hai using standard inference rules (Modus Ponens, Resolution) — ye inference-pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Modus Ponens: from P and P→Q, derive Q.
Resolution rule: from (A∨B) and (¬B∨C), derive (A∨C) — used heavily in logic-programming-style questions.
An argument (premises ⊢ conclusion) is VALID iff the conjunction of premises implies the conclusion is a TAUTOLOGY — i.e., whenever all premises are true, conclusion is forced true.
generalSolvingApproach: 2. Apply Modus Ponens/Resolution step by step, deriving new facts, until the target conclusion is reached (or shown unreachable).
3. To check validity of a claimed argument: assume ALL premises true, check if conclusion is FORCED true in every such case (truth table or direct reasoning).
variationsObserved: Predicate-logic flavored premises (monadic predicates with a constant) — same propositional reasoning skeleton, just with quantifiers stripped for a specific constant.
commonTraps: Applying Modus Ponens in the wrong direction (from Q and P→Q, you CANNOT derive P — affirming the consequent is a fallacy).

name: Definitions & Normal Forms (wff validity, CNF/DNF)
recognitionClueHinglish: 'Define validity of a wff', ya 'obtain the principal conjunctive normal form' poocha hai — ye definitional/normal-form-construction pattern hai, mostly old descriptive papers.
whatShouldComeToMind: CNF = AND of ORs. DNF = OR of ANDs. 'Principal'/canonical form includes every variable (or its negation) in every clause.
generalSolvingApproach: 2. For principal CNF: take every row where the formula is FALSE, write the OR-clause that is false exactly there, AND them all together.
3. For principal DNF: take every row where TRUE, write the AND-term true exactly there, OR them together.
commonTraps: Mixing up which rows to use for CNF (false rows) vs DNF (true rows).
